AeroHarp

A gesture-controlled AI music instrument. Record a hand gesture, and hear the music it generates. No keyboard, no MIDI controller, just a webcam and a model listening.

Fig. 0 — Raw Signal

Fig. 0 — a 21-point hand landmark map (MediaPipe), the raw signal this project performs on. Motion and shape become the control data for everything downstream.

Overview

What is this?

Most AI music tools work by typing a prompt and waiting for a finished clip, more like ordering a song than playing one. AeroHarp tries to close that gap. A webcam captures hand gestures, MediaPipe tracks hand landmarks, a classifier turns that into gesture and motion data, and that data controls Magenta RealTime 2 to generate music in response.

Hand position and motion map to continuous musical parameters like pitch and intensity, while distinct hand shapes trigger different musical styles. Because the real-time streaming version of Magenta RealTime 2 requires Apple Silicon hardware, AeroHarp runs in offline mode: gestures are recorded first, then processed through the pipeline to generate the corresponding audio, rather than responding live.

To build and test this, I recorded my own set of labeled hand gesture videos, since no existing dataset fit this task, trained a gesture classifier on top of MediaPipe's hand-tracking output, and measured classification accuracy against a simple pixel-motion baseline.

Results: Honestly better than I expected going in. The classifier hit 100% accuracy on clips it never saw during training, which crushed the dumb pixel-motion baseline sitting at 62.5%. It basically fixed the exact thing the baseline kept messing up (mixing up two closed-hand gestures that look similar if you're just tracking motion instead of actual hand shape). I also ran real recorded gestures all the way through the pipeline and the music genuinely does switch styles when the gesture changes, which was honestly a "wait, it's actually working" moment. The one thing I'll be real about: the classifier does great when I hold a pose still, but gets a lot shakier mid-transition, like while my hand is actively moving from one gesture to another. Makes sense in hindsight, since I only trained it on static held poses, no motion in between. Good problem to tackle if I keep building this out.
